title: Trump Removes State Department Inspector General Steve Linick
description_short: Trump removed State Department IG Steve Linick in May 2020 amid inquiries involving Mike Pompeo; motive remains disputed.
description_medium: Trump removed State Department Inspector General Steve Linick in May 2020 after Secretary Mike Pompeo recommended it. Linick’s office had two open Pompeo-related inquiries. Congressional leaders said the removal might be retaliatory; that was an allegation, not a finding. Pompeo denied knowing about the inquiry into alleged misuse of government resources, and lawmakers said in June that unanswered questions remained.
description_long:
On May 15, 2020, President Donald Trump removed State Department Inspector General Steve Linick. The Senate Foreign Relations Committee reported on May 16 that Senator Bob Menendez and House Foreign Affairs Chairman Eliot Engel had opened an inquiry into the removal and asked the White House, State Department, and inspector general’s office to preserve and provide records. They said Secretary of State Mike Pompeo had recommended Linick’s removal and described their understanding that it was connected to an investigation of possible wrongdoing by Pompeo. They called possible retaliation a concern; this was the lawmakers’ allegation, not a finding.

In a June 3 statement after Linick’s interview, congressional leaders said his office had two matters involving Pompeo open when he was removed. They described an inquiry into Pompeo’s 2019 emergency arms-sale declaration and an investigation into allegations that Pompeo and his wife misused government resources. The statement reported that Pompeo denied knowing about the misuse inquiry. It also said questions remained and the committees still sought interviews and documents. The May 16 announcement said the State Department had announced Stephen J. Akard would lead the inspector general’s office. These records document the oversight context and competing accounts; they do not establish retaliatory motive or the inquiries’ final findings.

supported_facts: On May 16, 2020, Senate and House committee leaders announced an investigation into Trump’s removal of Linick and requested records.
The lawmakers said Pompeo recommended the removal and alleged it may have been retaliation connected to an IG investigation.
The announcement identified Stephen J. Akard as the person State had announced would lead the OIG.

source_fact_map.limitation: The inquiry announcement records lawmakers’ stated understanding and allegation; it is not a finding that retaliation occurred.

supported_facts: The committee leaders requested records concerning the firing and open, pending, or incomplete IG investigations.
source_fact_map.quote: the lawmakers requested that administration officials preserve all records related to the firing and turn information over to the committees by Friday, May 22.
source_fact_map.limitation: This announcement describes a request, not the committee’s ultimate findings.

supported_facts: The source attributes the recommendation to Pompeo and describes lawmakers’ understanding of a connection to an investigation.
source_fact_map.quote: Reports indicate that Secretary Pompeo personally made the recommendation to fire Mr. Linick, and it is our understanding that he did so because the Inspector General had opened an investigation into wrongdoing by Secretary Pompeo himself.
source_fact_map.limitation: The causal account is attributed to the lawmakers and reports they cited.

supported_facts: The department had announced Stephen J. Akard would lead the Office of Inspector General.
source_fact_map.quote: information about Stephen J. Akard, whom the State Department has announced will lead the OIG
source_fact_map.limitation: The announcement identifies the planned leader; it does not establish the later tenure or performance of the successor.

supported_facts: Linick’s office had two matters involving Pompeo open at the time of removal.
One concerned Pompeo’s 2019 emergency arms-sale declaration; another concerned alleged misuse of government resources by Pompeo and his wife.
source_fact_map.quote: Mr. Linick confirmed that at the time of his firing, there was an ongoing investigation into allegations of misuse of government resources by Secretary Pompeo and his wife.
source_fact_map.limitation: The source reports the committee’s summary of Linick’s testimony and describes the misuse as an allegation.

supported_facts: Pompeo denied knowing about the alleged misuse inquiry.
As of June 3, committee leaders said unanswered questions and requests for further interviews and documents remained.
source_fact_map.quote: On May 18, three days after Mr. Linick was fired at Secretary Pompeo’s recommendation, Pompeo denied knowing about this investigation in an interview with the Washington Post.
source_fact_map.limitation: The statement reports Pompeo’s denial and does not resolve the competing accounts.

supported_facts: The committees reported that questions remained and sought more witness interviews and documents as of June 3, 2020.
source_fact_map.quote: We still have many unanswered questions, and today’s testimony makes it all the more critical that the Administration immediately comply with outstanding requests for additional witness interviews and documents.
source_fact_map.limitation: This establishes the inquiry’s status as described on June 3, not its ultimate later disposition.
